newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German state to sell rest of Lufthansa.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German state to sell rest of Lufthansa.

text.p: The German government on Thursday reaffirmed its commitment to sell its remaining stake in Lufthansa AG after reaching a deal with the European Commission that would allow foreigners to buy into the airline without gaining control of the flag carrier.

But the finance ministry said it had no firm plans yet for the sale of the remaining 36 percent stake worth some $2 billion after Bonn reached the pact with Brussels with assurances that the sale would not discriminate against foreign shareholders.
"We want to get out of Lufthansa completely, all the way down to zero," Eberhard Rolle, head of the ministry's department for government holdings, told Reuters.
Shares in Lufthansa slumped on the announcement, falling 55 pfennigs to 20.00 marks in morning bourse trade while the broader market 30-share DAX index posted modest gains.

European Union Commissioner Neil Kinnock sent a letter to German transport minister Matthias Wissmann accepting Wissmann's proposal for a transition period governing the sales, a German transport ministry spokesman said on Thursday.

The European Commission wanted assurances that ownership of Lufthansa would remain with Germans and finding a way to monitor that was difficult. The transport ministry agreed that it would have the transition period during the sale, allowing the government to buy back shares if the German majority in Lufthansa is threatened.
The sell-off had been delayed by international air law which requires fLag carriers to demonstrate that national shareholders hold majority stakes if they are to retain their rights.

Many of about 200 bilateral air traffic agreements between Germany and other countries stipulate that Lufthansa must remain in the hands of German investors, a condition not easily maintained if the shares are traded freely.

Wissmann's proposal would allow the German government to buy back shares if the German majority in Lufthansa were threatened, a ministry spokesman said. But Bonn's right to conduct such "last in-first out" purchases would be limited, Wissman said in a statement issued by the ministry.

The German finance ministry has said it would like to complete Lufthansa's privatisation by the end of 1997, a delay from earlier goals for 1996 due to next week's massive public offering of shares in telephone Deutsche Telekom.
"It is unlikely to happen this year, Christmas is just a month away. But we will begin making preparations next week, after Telekom," he said.
Rolle said the government welcomed the decision to allow the sale but said Bonn must study the conditions placed on the sale before deciding how and when to sell its shares.
He added that it was not yet clear what conditions or restrictions Bonn would face from Brussels for the sale.

"We have to study the document first. We are not certain yet how this will be done technically, whether we can sell it all at once or in parts. But our goal remains the same, to get out of Lufthansa completely," he said.

Lufthansa was partially sold off to private investors in 1994. The goverment retained the 36 percent stake, which the cash-strapped finance ministry -- seeking to whip Germany's finances into shape for European currency union -- is keen to sell to raise about 3.00 billion marks ($2 billion).
Also on Thursday, Lufthansa chief executive Juergen Weber said in a newspaper interview that the airline expects to earn about as much in 1996 as it did in 1995.

Weber told the Frankfurter Rundschau newspaper that, assuming that things go as planned, the company's profit would "at least not be far from the 1995 result". But he said the return on sales would "not be satisfactory".
The Frankfurt-based airline in 1995 reported a group profit from ordinary activities of 756.3 million marks while the return on sales was 3.8 percent.
